Review Body:
"We now know that there is another possible response to threat, which our scans aren't capable of measuring. Some people simply go into denial: Their bodies register the threat, but their conscious minds go on as if nothing has happened. However, even though the mind may learn to ignore the messages from the emotional brain, the alarm signals don't stop. The emotional brain keeps working, and stress hormones keep sending signals to the muscles to tense for action or immobilize in collapse. The physical effects on the organs go on unabated until they demand notice when they are expressed as illness. Medications, drugs, and alcohol can also temporarily dull or obliterate unbearable sensations and feelings. But the body continues to keep the score."

I’ve dedicated January 2025 to reading books that have been languishing on my TBR list. The Body Keeps the Score is the first of four that I’ve chosen. I became interested in reading this after it was recommend by a podcaster I regularly listen to. I started and stopped it a couple of times in 2024. I wasn’t fully prepared for how dense it is.

The book begins with a history of the development of the modern medical approach to mental suffering and includes many examples from the author's own education and practice. There are a lot of scientific details and uncomfortable accounts of child abuse, sexual assaults, and wartime atrocities.

Things I liked:

The chapter on the body-brain connections, particularly the description of fight, flight, or freeze and the reasons behind the physical manifestations we experience during these states.

The part that discusses the paths to recovery. It was interesting to read about various treatment modalities.

Things I didn't like:

This is a long book and I kind of got lost in all the words. I feel like the word count could have been cut in half and it would have been a much more understandable read.

The author speaks of repressed memories as settled fact, but they have not been supported by research and are not universally accepted as true.

The details of various traumas, particularly child sexual abuse, seemed unnecessary and could be triggering for some individuals. I feel like this was an unwise inclusion in a book geared to people who have experienced trauma.

There is no discussion of the resiliency of humans. If you were to believe this book, everyone who has experienced trauma would be unable to function without professional help, but many do recover on their own and go on to live healthy, well adjusted lives.

I am glad I read this book to have an idea of what everyone is talking about and it did give me some things to think about, but I am surprised that it is so popular with such high reviews. It was a slog for me and I'm glad to be done reading it.

I had severe anxiety myself after my children were born and ultimately found my way out of it by going through it deeply and wholeheartedly. And the greatest, most powerful, and truest way to healing is with God. Once you open yourself to spiritual healing through the Holy Spirit and literally ask God to help you (and truly believe in that help from God), you can leave your mind problems behind. I personally found the writings of Eckhart Tolle extremely helpful when I was going through the worst of my anxiety over a decade ago. He is brilliant and simple. Hi I am still listening to this book. Part 1 about human trauma was fascinating. I loved it.

However, I'm a biologist with a background in animal behavior and Part II leans hard into a ton of misinformation about other animals and animal behavior generally. For example, the author repeatedly says that all mammals are social and implies that reptiles are never social and don't ever play or get bored. All mammals are not social. Many are quite solitary. Likewise, go to youtube and you can see tortoises playing with balls etc. And many snakes hang out in colonies at least part of the time. Animals play. Spiders dream. And the assumption that a "lower" animal in a plexiglass box is fine is just wrong. Bottom line, when the author gets away from actual people and trauma and starts talking about theory based on his weak understanding of organismal biology, he's out of his depth. I am hoping the rest of the book is more focused on human trauma. I'll hopefully be able to revise my review, but wanted to say this while it's fresh.

While it’s true your body will remember all your traumas, The most helpful book to integrate your trauma experiences with your adult mind is a workbook you can use on yourself, if the traumas were not overwhelming and totally repressed. The book is by Ingeborg Bosch PsyD “Past Reality Integration: 3 Steps to Mastering the Art of Conscious Living”. This book can change your life if you do the 15 min/day prescribed work.

Dutch psychologist Ingeborg, built on the work of Alice Miller and Arthur Janov to created a simple direct process to safely access your repressed childhood feelings as an adult. She completed the process herself and you can see her results by watching her on youtube and TedTalks. Everyone could use this, you may need the help of a therapist if your trauma was intense or long lasting.

Your feelings are the the keys to your health; Only therapists who have experienced the integration of repressed childhood feelings themselves have the necessary empathy to help others. The therapist’s emotional evolution is critical to your outcome. You want a therpist who has recovered from serious abuse.

I’ve recovered from the desth of my mother at 5yo, sexual Priest abuse, malignant narcissism child beatings and degradation from a ‘care giver’.

I had 6 years of talk therapy, I’ve read 40 psychology books, my wife is a family therapist, and I had a traumatic brain injury where my built up emotional rationalizations where erased—the injury forced me to rehabilitate my psyche.

Review Body:
Yes, there are some good parts to this book. However, we continue to learn more.

What is CTE?

According to the Boston University CTE Center, Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) is a degenerative brain disease found in athletes, military veterans, and others with a history of repetitive brain trauma. Most of what we have learned about CTE has come from the research of Dr. Ann McKee, director of the VA-BU-CLF Brain Bank. In CTE, a protein called tau misfolds and malfunctions, causes other proteins to misfold, and sets off a chain reaction where this malfunctioning tau slowly spreads throughout the brain, killing brain cells. CTE has been seen in people as young as 17, but symptoms do not generally begin appearing until years after the onset of head impacts.

There are times, when people, particularly war veterans who have been near a blast or an explosion or bomb, or football players who have also suffered head impact/injuries.

It may be PTSD, but it may also be CTE, either one, the other, or a combination of both.

It is sad when we keep attempting various psychological approaches to a brain which may have suffered damage which cannot be healed by psychological approaches. Or, the person may have both PTSD and CTE.

It is vital that you find someone who understands CTE, will listen and take this seriously.

I listened to a young lady sorrowfully saying her boyfriend would have angry outbursts, then cry and indicate that he did not know why and how sorry he was. I asked her about some of his history, specifically having been near blasts, such as war, or football. He had been a star college football player, having taken many hits and rattles to the head/brain. He needed to be checked by someone who is familiar and understands CTE.

There is very little known, or which can be done after the damage has been done. However, it is not fair to a veteran to spend years in therapy, thinking that they have PTSD, when they have the physical damage, such as CTE.

If veterans are found to have irreparable CTE, they must be diagnosed and receive help, diagnosis, and, if they are unable to function in order to support themselves and or their family, they must be compensated, which, as we know, the VA may not like or help and years of research may be needed before necessary support is provided.

Also, there is not much known yet as to how to help or repair the damage. The only research I have read to date, is the possibility of hyperbaric oxygen therapy for treating CTE and this is still experimental.

The most important thing we can do is prevention. To protect the brain whenever possible. Had I known about CTE prior to my children playing high school football, I would never have allowed them to play football. It is not worth the possible damage.

I have also known children children and their families who have been guided to psychological counseling. One little boy, from about 5 years of age had horrible back pain. He would tell his family, they would take him to the Dr.. His father was very tall and broad, the Dr. would tell the parents that he was just experiencing some growing pains. If they needed it, they could provide some psychological counseling. It was not until about 6 years later that this child was continuing to have terrible pain. The father slammed his fist down on the table and demanded a scan, as this child was suffering. They finally agreed to a scan. The boy had a tumor wrapping around and up his spine. It was heartbreaking. Surgery was performed, then he was in a wheelchair. Then a few years later, after multiple surgeries, he said enough and passed away, shortly after graduating. I am heart broken as well, wondering if I could have insisted as well, when he was young. I saw how much pain he was in, even when walking as early as 5 years old.

Then there was a middle school girl who had on going stomach pains, the Dr. insisted that she was a hypochondriac and had the child and family attend counseling. It was not until a couple of years later that the girl was in middle school and passed out. She was rushed to the ER where it was found that she had a tumor the size of a bowling ball. It was wrapped all over her internal organs and after removing it, she had to take hormone pills and was told she would never be able to have children.

Then there was a woman whose daughter had stomach pains. The mother took her to the Dr.. The Dr. said she was probably just experiencing some hormonal issues as she would probably soon be starting her period. About a month later, the mother called me, indicating that she was in the ER, her daughter had been in pain, then passed out. The terrible pains had been due to a gallbladder attack. The middle school age girl had a gallbladder that was similar to that of a very elderly person.

LISTEN TO PEOPLE AND TAKE THEM SERIOUSLY BEYOND PSYCHOLOGICAL COUNSELING!!!

Just because a medical Dr. does not know what is wrong, does not mean there is nothing wrong. Medical Dr'ss need to learn to say, "I don't know." !!!

Also, when you can, if you think something is wrong, and the Dr. guides you to psychological counseling, get another opinion!!!

I also have a friend who is a Dr. whose husband was diagnosed with a heart ailment. He underwent a procedure to fix it, but when put under, they did not find what they suspected to be the problem. She turned to her medical community, indicating her husbands symptoms. A number of other Dr.'s indicated that his racing heart may be due to sleep apnea. He was waking up with a racing heart as his body thought, without oxygen he may die. The Dr. who thought it was a heart issue, upon not finding the problem, tried to guide him to psychological counseling. His problem is was solved with a C-pap machine.

We are all going to die, so please, in between whatever appointments you have, make some fun memories and have a good time! Break out the good china and live it up, with friends and family!

I wish you joy and good health and good help when you need it on your journey!
